summary: MOOSEDev stores architectural decisions, lessons, constraints and rationales as typed records (two small OWL/SHACL ontologies, 20 classes, 51 properties) with lifecycle status and supersession links in a knowledge graph on Trivyn's proprietary MOOSE neurosymbolic engine, exposed to coding agents over MCP. On a third-party documentation corpus (835 typed records) the author reports near-complete answers (0.98-1.00) on set-completeness, negation and supersession questions versus 6-27% for mem0 top-k retrieval and parity on plain relevance; a commit-history bootstrap and a 21-day in-house live trial are described. Every evaluation is run by the vendor on its own product.

claims.claim: The typed graph returns the expected answer set essentially in full (0.98-1.00) on supersession, set-completeness and negation questions, versus 6-27% for mem0
claims.evidence: Unnumbered table in §3: B2 1.00/0.98/0.98, mem0 0.18/0.06/0.27, flat docs 0.08/0.00/0.12. The number of questions per task class is never reported. Part of the ground truth is 'SPARQL-derived sets', i.e. computed from the graph being evaluated. The GPT-5.4-mini judge was validated only by reproducing the graph condition's own strict-match score (mean of 3 passes; an earlier unlogged pass moved cells by up to 0.12). Top-k retrievers cannot enumerate sets or prove absence by construction, so the gap is largely definitional.

claims.claim: Relevance recall and token cost are largely equivalent between the graph and vector memory
claims.evidence: §3: graph coverage 0.82 at ~35k tokens vs mem0 0.67-0.90 at ~40k (a range, no n). The scale study (50-634 records) puts the graph ahead at every size (hit@5 0.84 vs 0.60 at the largest; slope CI spans zero), which does not match 'parity'. SPARQL completeness answers cost 78k-167k tokens vs ~35k for targeted retrieval.

claims.claim: Supersession filtering keeps current-guidance answers current
claims.evidence: §3: the graph is current in all 40 trials (4 reversal pairs x 4 models x 2 regimes = 32 cells; the allocation behind 40 is unexplained). It is current by construction because superseded records are filtered. mem0 also scored 100% on the reversal tested, and only BM25 with the superseded content pushed into the prompt failed (1/13) on one pair. So no advantage over the production comparator is shown.
claims.location: §3 Parity on retrieval, currency by construction

claims.claim: Commit-by-commit history bootstrap recovers historical decision structure
claims.evidence: §4: one sentence, 'recovered seven real supersession chains' on the author's own repository; no precision or recall and no external repository. The lessons section admits a misleading commit message poisoned a bootstrapped rationale.

claims.claim: A pre-registered live trial shows the graph assisting in daily use
claims.evidence: §4: 71 unprompted record-citing assists vs 38 logged misses in 21 days on two company codebases (35 of 38 misses in one thinly bootstrapped project). Self-logged by the vendor; no registry ID or link; the registered readout (monthly graph-vs-cold trend) is not yet reported.

patterns.note: Comparison: typed graph memory vs mem0 (production vector memory), BM25 over the same content flattened, flat docs, and no memory. The graph wins on structural questions (enumerate, absence, supersession) and ties on simple relevance. Ground truth is partly SPARQL-derived from the graph itself, the per-class n is unreported, there is one agent model family, and the vendor ran everything.

Typed ontology records vs the same content without structure (B1-rag BM25: set-overlap F1 0.90 vs 0.34 public, 0.94 vs 0.25 private) is an isolating structure-vs-content comparison. The cheap alternative is never tested: ADR markdown with status/superseded-by fields that an agent can grep or parse. The author concedes the advantage depends on correct typed capture, and flat capture drops to free-text parity (§4 Barriers).
A knowledge graph over decisions about code, not the code itself. Same comparison as P09/P39. Completeness via SPARQL costs 78k-167k tokens vs ~35k for targeted retrieval.
mem0 embedding retrieval surfaces only 6-27% of complete answer sets because it returns a ranked slice, but it ties the graph on relevance and on the one reversal tested for currency.
Exposed through four MCP tool groups. The author notes MCP is passive: the agent decides when to call, which favours higher-tier models.
Recovering the rationale behind reversals whose earlier approach was deleted from the tree, so it cannot be reconstructed from the code. Measured only as uncontrolled live-trial assist counts.

Motivated by 'comprehension debt' (Naur). The claim that structured memory reduces it is explicitly untested (live-trial readout pending), and what is measured is agent recall, not developer comprehension.

Strict LLM judge validated only against the system's own condition. The author reports nearly shipping a 20-point win for his own system that turned out to be a grading artifact, which caught a judge problem but shows how fragile the measurement is.
Records carry 'affects component' edges to code entities, but link correctness is not evaluated.

methodology.sample: 835 typed records (553 mem0 memories) from the CodeGraph docs, plus an unnamed private corpus. Number of questions per task class not reported. Scale study 50-634 records; currency study 4 reversal pairs, 40 trials; live trial on 2 company codebases, 16 reference points, 21 days
methodology.baselines: B0 no memory; B1-notes flat docs; B1-mem0 with its native capture; B1-rag BM25 over the graph content flattened. No agent+grep over typed ADR files; no plain triple store + SPARQL without the proprietary engine
methodology.models: One CLI agent configuration, GPT-5.x family; judge GPT-5.4-mini (same family); currency study four unnamed models; engine uses an 8-32B LLM at narrow points
methodology.variance: Mean of three judge passes; CI only on the scale-study slope; no CIs or per-item run counts for the main table
methodology.ablations: B1-rag isolates structure vs content; no ablation of SHACL validation, the supersession filter, or the engine itself
methodology.contamination_controls: Third-party corpus; ground truth 'from primary sources or SPARQL-derived sets' (the latter computed from the evaluated graph)

standards.peer_review: NeSy 2026 Industry Track (5 pages), PMLR vol. 284
standards.artifacts: Benchmark harness, CodeGraph corpus export and public-corpus transcripts at github.com/Trivyn/moosedev (Apache-2.0, public). MOOSE engine proprietary; private-corpus transcripts withheld
standards.preregistration: Claimed for benchmark verdicts and the live trial; no registry ID or link given

biases.detail: Vendor's proprietary engine, vendor-designed task classes, vendor-authored ground truth and judge configuration, compared against a competitor product.

Task classes (enumerate all, prove absence, follow supersession) are exactly what a SPARQL-queryable store does and a top-k retriever cannot do by construction; part of the gold sets is SPARQL-derived from the graph under test.
Judge validated only by reproducing the graph condition's own score; no human agreement on baseline outputs; judge from the same GPT-5.x family as the agent.
Main matrix uses one agent model family; author concedes 'we evaluated one agent family'.
No per-class n, no CIs on the headline table.
Engine is proprietary; private-corpus transcripts withheld, so the head-to-head cannot be re-run independently, only re-graded.
Live-trial assists and misses are logged by the vendor on its own codebases.
Currency on 4 reversal pairs; live trial 21 days, 16 reference points, 2 codebases.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: MOOSEDev and the proprietary MOOSE neurosymbolic engine plus Trivyn ontology workbench (author's company), against mem0
coi.detail: Vendor evaluates its own proprietary product favourably against a competitor with no independent replication. Partly mitigated by public-corpus transcripts that allow re-grading and by candid disclosure of near-miss measurement errors.

verdict_reason: Vendor-run evaluation of a proprietary engine with unreported per-class sample sizes, partly circular ground truth, a judge validated only against the system's own score, and one model family. The useful point, that top-k vector memory cannot enumerate, prove absence or follow supersession while typed records with status and supersedes links can, is close to definitional and should enter the KB as a design hypothesis, not as evidence.
applicability: For the 'capture knowledge back' step: keep decisions and constraints as typed records with status and supersedes links, and answer 'which accepted decisions affect component X', 'what replaced Y' and 'is there any rule about Z' with deterministic queries, not vector top-k memory. For a Java team spanning several repositories this needs no OWL engine: ADR markdown with front-matter (type, status, superseded_by, affects) in each repo or a shared decisions repo, validated by a schema check and queried by grep or a small CLI, gives the enumeration and supersession filtering. Tie capture to the PR/spec workflow, because the paper's own stated barrier is capture discipline. Agents only call a passive MCP tool when they decide to, so push relevant records when an agent or newcomer touches a component. Re-measure on your own repos; this evidence is vendor-only and GPT-only.

conflicts_with.detail: LongMemEval-V2 finds a coding agent searching raw files is near the best memory system and well ahead of RAG. Here the flat-docs agent condition scores 0.00-0.12 on structural questions, which suggests MOOSEDev's flat-file baseline may be under-tooled, or that the result depends heavily on task class.
